newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Baht devaluation seen boosting Thai sugar sector.
newsitem.headline: Baht devaluation seen boosting Thai sugar sector.

text.p: Thai sugar farmers are likely to benefit in the short-term from the recent float of the baht, in a sector where output next year is expected to fall sharply due to a severe drought, industry sources said on Thursday.

"The de facto devaluation of the baht will make life easier for sugarcane farmers. The industry stands to gain," Saeng Sanguanruang, general manager of the Thai Cane and Sugar Corp Ltd, told a sugar conference on the Indonesian tourist island of Bali.
He later told Reuters that a severe drought sweeping across many parts of the Southeast Asian country was expected to cause a 15-percent fall in sugar production next year.

"The production is most likely going to be reduced by 15 percent because of the drought, which is quite widespread," he said. "Maybe different regions might not be impacted in the same way, but largely the drought is widespread."
Sanguanruang said Thailand was expected to produce 5.8 million tonnes of sugar in 1997, down from 6.0 million tonnes in 1996.
He declined to give details on the baht's possible impact on sugar exports, saying it was a sensitive subject.
Peter Baron of the International Sugar Organisation (ISO) said the weaker baht should strengthen the position of the Thai sugar sector in the short term.
"In the long run you don't know. That's the problem with currency movements. That is a risk which you can normally take on the market by hedging," he told Reuters.
"(The devaluation) will give you more baht (for dollars)...it is obviously a short-term advantage, but how it will turn out in the long run is another question," he said.

Other industry sources said Thailand was not expected to benefit substantially this year from the weakening of the baht against the U.S. dollar following its de facto devaluation last month because most of the export shipments had been committed.
"I think the benefits will come only next year," one Asian sugar company executive said. "The Thais are getting more baht now for each U.S. dollar and export prices are quoted in dollars."
Thailand's Sanguanruang told the conference that Thai domestic sugar consumption had soared to 1.58 million tonnes in 1996 from about 631,000 tonnes in 1983.

"With a small annual growth of population of around 1.4 percent, the increase...was due largely to a rise of income resulting in a substantial rise in per capita consumption which more than doubled to 26.29 kgs during the period," he said.

He said exports rose dramatically to 4.4 million tonnes in 1996 from 1.5 million tonnes in 1983. "The proportion of sugar exported was about 73 percent in 1996 and has averaged about 70 percent of total output during the last five years."

Sanguanruang said traditional export markets for Thai sugar are Japan, China, South Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia, but added that new destinations in the Middle East and Africa had opened up in recent years.
He said demand for Thai sugar to the year 2000 would continue to be strong, adding that Australia was the only major competitor in the region.
"With low production costs and efficient export handling, Australia will continue to be an indomitable competitor, unless Thailand's costs could be reduced substantially," he said.
